boardAlignment.summary: Central and peripheral nervous-system divisions, including somatic and autonomic systems.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord and integrates information and coordinates responses.
The peripheral nervous system comprises nerves outside the brain and spinal cord and connects the central nervous system with sensory receptors, muscles, organs and glands.
The somatic nervous system carries sensory information to the central nervous system and motor commands to skeletal muscles.
The autonomic nervous system regulates largely involuntary functions of internal organs and glands and includes sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: The sympathetic division generally mobilises resources for action, while the parasympathetic division supports restoration and routine maintenance; their effects are coordinated rather than simple all-or-none opposites.
evaluationAndLimits: The division labels are useful organising categories, but nervous-system regulation is integrated across central and peripheral structures rather than operating as isolated subsystems.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Autonomic does not mean completely independent of the brain; autonomic regulation is centrally coordinated.
The peripheral nervous system includes both sensory and motor pathways, not only motor nerves.

boardAlignment.summary: Sensory, relay and motor neurons, synaptic transmission, neurotransmitters, excitation and inhibition.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Sensory neurons transmit information from sensory receptors toward the central nervous system; motor neurons transmit commands from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles.
Interneurons connect neurons within the central nervous system. The AQA term relay neuron is retained as qualification framing for this connecting function.

An action potential is an electrical signal propagated along a neuron. At a chemical synapse, arrival of the action potential triggers neurotransmitter release from the presynaptic terminal into the synaptic cleft.
Neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the postsynaptic cell and can produce excitatory or inhibitory effects depending on the transmitter, receptor and cell context.
Excitatory postsynaptic effects tend to depolarise the receiving cell and increase the likelihood of firing; inhibitory effects tend to hyperpolarise it and reduce that likelihood.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Neural output reflects summation and integration of multiple excitatory and inhibitory inputs rather than a single synapse determining whether the neuron fires.

Glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system and GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter, while their effects still depend on receptor mechanisms and circuit context.
evaluationAndLimits: Labels such as excitatory and inhibitory describe effects on postsynaptic signalling; they should not be treated as fixed descriptions of a neurotransmitter in every biological context.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Neurotransmission across a chemical synapse is chemical, while signal propagation along an axon is electrical.
A relay neuron is not a third peripheral pathway equivalent to sensory and motor neurons; it functions within central neural circuits.

revisionSynthesis: Revision uses the AQA label 'relay neuron' as course alignment while explaining the independently sourced interneuron function rather than treating protected specification wording as teaching corpus.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: The endocrine system is a network of glands that release hormones into the bloodstream, allowing chemical signals to act on target tissues with appropriate receptors.
Hormonal signalling is generally slower in onset and longer lasting than rapid neural signalling.
The pituitary gland interacts with hypothalamic control and helps regulate other endocrine glands; other major glands include the thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas and gonads.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Endocrine and nervous systems interact continuously; the hypothalamus is an important interface between neural regulation and endocrine output.
evaluationAndLimits: Hormones can influence behaviour and physiology but their effects depend on receptors, feedback systems and wider biological and environmental context.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Hormonal effects are not independent of the nervous system.
A hormone does not affect every cell equally; target-cell receptors matter.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: The acute fight-or-flight response prepares the body to respond rapidly to perceived threat through coordinated autonomic and endocrine activity.
Sympathetic activation increases physiological readiness, including cardiovascular and respiratory changes, while the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline into the bloodstream.
After the immediate challenge passes, parasympathetic activity contributes to restoring routine physiological conditions.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: The sympathetic-adrenal-medullary response is rapid; longer-lasting stress responses can also involve the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and cortisol, which should not be collapsed into the immediate adrenaline response.
evaluationAndLimits: Fight or flight is a useful description of acute mobilisation, but real stress responses vary across situations and individuals and may include freezing, vigilance and other response patterns.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Adrenaline is a hormone released into the bloodstream as part of the acute response; it is not the sole cause of every stress-related change.
Fight or flight is not the same as the complete longer-term stress response.

boardAlignment.summary: Brain-study methods: fMRI, EEG, event-related potentials and post-mortem examination.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Functional magnetic resonance imaging estimates changes associated with neural activity through blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals, providing relatively high spatial resolution but indirect and comparatively slow measures of neural activity.
Electroencephalography records electrical activity from electrodes at the scalp, providing high temporal resolution but limited ability to localise deep or precise neural sources.

An event-related potential is derived from EEG by aligning recordings to repeated occurrences of a defined event and averaging across trials so activity consistently time-locked to that event can be identified.
Post-mortem examination studies brain tissue after death and can reveal structural or pathological features unavailable from some in-vivo methods.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: ERP components can be described using properties such as timing/latency, amplitude, polarity and scalp distribution; interpretation requires careful experimental control and signal processing.
The four methods answer different questions and involve different temporal, spatial, causal and practical trade-offs.
evaluationAndLimits: fMRI blood-oxygen signals are indirect correlates of neural activity and should not be interpreted as direct recordings of neurons firing.
EEG and ERP signals are vulnerable to noise and artefacts, and scalp recordings blur the spatial origin of activity.
Post-mortem evidence is observational and can be affected by pre-existing illness, treatment, cause of death and the absence of a living behavioural measure.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: An ERP is not a separate brain signal unrelated to EEG; it is extracted from EEG data through event-related analysis.
High spatial resolution does not mean fMRI establishes causation between a brain region and behaviour.

revisionSynthesis: Revision presents the methods comparatively so learners can explain both what each measures and why method choice changes the strength and type of inference available.

boardAlignment.summary: Functional localisation and hemispheric lateralisation, including cortical centres, Broca and Wernicke, split-brain research, plasticity and functional recovery after trauma.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Functional localisation is the principle that some psychological and behavioural functions depend disproportionately on particular neural regions, while complex functions usually involve distributed interacting systems.

The primary motor cortex is strongly involved in voluntary movement; the primary somatosensory cortex processes bodily touch and related somatic information; primary visual cortex receives visual input; and primary auditory cortex processes auditory input.
Broca’s area is classically associated with language production and Wernicke’s area with language comprehension, with both usually lateralised toward the left hemisphere in most people.
Hemispheric lateralisation refers to relative specialisation of functions between the two cerebral hemispheres rather than one hemisphere controlling an entire personality style.
Neuroplasticity is the nervous system’s capacity to change its structure or functional organisation through development, experience, learning or response to damage.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: The corpus callosum normally transfers information between hemispheres. Split-brain surgery severs this major connection, allowing researchers such as Gazzaniga and colleagues to study processing that is temporarily confined to one hemisphere.

In classic split-brain tasks, information presented to the left visual field is initially processed by the right hemisphere and may not be verbally named when interhemispheric transfer is unavailable, while non-verbal responses controlled by that hemisphere can remain possible.
After brain injury, functional recovery can involve reorganisation of surviving networks, changes in synaptic connections and rehabilitation-supported recruitment of alternative pathways.
evaluationAndLimits: Localisation evidence from lesions and split-brain cases can be powerful but individual brains differ, lesions can affect networks beyond a single focal site and small specialist samples limit simple generalisation.
Plasticity creates capacity for adaptation but does not guarantee full recovery; outcome varies with injury location and severity, age, time, rehabilitation and wider individual factors.
Modern neuroscience supports functional specialisation alongside network interaction, so a rigid one-function-one-area account is too simple.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Split-brain findings do not support popular claims that people are globally 'left-brained' or 'right-brained'.
Plasticity is not always beneficial and should not be equated with guaranteed recovery.
Broca and Wernicke findings illustrate important language specialisation but language depends on wider neural networks.

supports: functional recovery after traumatic brain injury
sourceEvidence.caution: Recovery examples are illustrative; do not infer that comparable recovery occurs after every injury.

revisionSynthesis: Revision combines localisation, lateralisation and plasticity as related but distinct concepts: specialised neural organisation can be demonstrated while the same nervous system retains capacity for adaptive reorganisation.
AQA’s exact topic labels remain qualification framing; the explanatory model is independently synthesised from commercially reusable neuroscience sources.
